body.text: Queensland LNP government dismisses expert national puberty blocker advice as 'ideological'
In short:
An advocacy group has called on the Queensland government to reconsider puberty blocker ban.
A national review found the treatment should remain an option for trans and gender diverse people under 18.
What's next?
The National Health and Medical Research Council is due to release national guidelines in 2028.

Queensland's deputy premier has rejected the advice of the nation's independent expert health advisory body on the topic of puberty blockers, saying the federal government has taken an "ideological view" on the controversial issue.

Earlier this week, the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC), which is an independent statutory agency, released its interim advice on the use of puberty suppressants in the care of trans and gender diverse people aged under 18, finding the treatment should remain an option.
The NHMRC report said that "based on a shared decision" between young people, parents and clinicians, the medications "can be considered" for a young person who wants puberty suppression.

Described as Australia's "pre-eminent" medical research body by the federal health minister, the NHMRC said healthcare professionals should conduct a comprehensive health assessment before prescribing puberty blockers, and there should be multidisciplinary input and appropriate monitoring.

The 45-page NHMRC report explained that its recommendation for the use of puberty blockers was "conditional" because different treatment options may be appropriate for different individuals and the "overall certainty of available evidence is low".
"Conditional recommendations are more common than strong recommendations in clinical practice guidelines," the report said.
The use of puberty blockers, which suppress sex hormones, pausing puberty, has become highly contested, with some countries including the United Kingdom restricting their use.
The Queensland response

Last December the Queensland government announced its ban on puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for new young trans patients in the public system would continue until at least 2031, when the results of a British medical trial are due.
Publicly funded puberty blockers are also prohibited in the Northern Territory.

On Monday, a spokesperson for Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls rejected the NHMRC's new advice, saying the government's position "remains unchanged, and we will continue to prioritise the health, safety and wellbeing of young Queenslanders".
"The Queensland government has already undertaken an independent review and made a clear decision on the provision of these treatments in our public hospitals," the spokesperson said in a statement.
Today the state's deputy premier Jarrod Bleijie went further, saying the government did not believe "those children should be taking puberty blockers".
"That's why we stopped it and we're not changing our position on that, despite the federal government taking an ideological view on it," Mr Bleijie said.
"We're taking a science-based view and we're not changing our position on that."
Advocacy group Parents of Trans Kids Speak Out has implored the LNP government to reconsider.
"At a national level, the peak health organisation, NHMRC, have found puberty blockers are considered a safe and appropriate option for trans and gender diverse young people under 18," they said.
"Meanwhile, here in Queensland, our children are still banned from accessing this safe and appropriate health care."
The mother of a 15-year-old trans girl has told ABC News she was "incredibly pleased" with the NHMRC's report.
"They've suggested a cautious, conservative process and I firmly believe that we should be following it in Queensland," she said.
"That will hopefully ensure that the action that's been taken in Queensland and the Northern Territory doesn't spread to any other states."
The mum questioned why the Crisafulli government was waiting for the results of a UK study.
"For goodness sakes, why are they not listening to Australian doctors and allied health professionals who specialise in the area?"
The woman, who did not want to be named to protect her child's identity, said the ban meant Queensland parents had to pay for costly medication.
"It's incredibly expensive to go through the private system so that's money that you can't spend on other things like your rent and your food."
'Highly charged public debate' about trans care

Yesterday federal Health Minister Mark Butler told journalists he respected the right of the Queensland and Northern Territory governments to make decisions about the public health care available for trans children.
"They're accountable to voters in their community," he said.
Mr Butler said the NHMRC had been reviewing evidence and developing clinical guidelines "for literally decades".

"Rather than have this very highly charged public debate driven and settled by opinion writers in our newspapers, I thought it was important that families and the community have the confidence that clinicians are using the most up-to-date, highest quality clinical guidelines," he said.
The NHMRC's puberty blocker advice is open for public consultation.
Its full national guidelines for the care of young trans and gender diverse people are due in 2028.
